articles.title: The Man Who Learned to Answer Softly
articles.dek: Peter once met a simple question with a sword and then a curse. Years later he told a suffering church how to answer the world, and every word he chose sounds like a man who remembered the courtyard.
articles.quote: Hope that has set Christ apart in the heart can afford to speak softly.
articles.body:
On the evening of October 10, 2008, Senator John McCain stood in a crowded hall in Lakeville, Minnesota. He was a few weeks from the end of a hard presidential race, and he was behind in the polls. The room was full of his own supporters, and many of them were angry and afraid of the man running against him. When the microphone reached an older woman near the front, she said she could not trust Barack Obama, and then she started repeating a false rumor about who he really was. A candidate who was losing could have used that moment. The crowd was ready, and a nod or a shrug would have cost him nothing.

McCain was already shaking his head. He gently took the microphone back from her and said, "No, ma'am. He's a decent family man, citizen, that I just happen to have disagreements with on fundamental issues, and that's what this campaign's all about." A few minutes earlier he had told the same crowd that Obama was a decent person they did not need to be scared of as president, and some of his own supporters booed him. He said it anyway. When McCain died ten years later, the man he had defended stood in Washington National Cathedral and spoke in his honor. Whatever anyone thinks of either man's politics, that moment at the microphone is still remembered as a picture of someone holding firm convictions while speaking of an opponent with respect.

The apostle Peter wrote to Christians who needed that same picture, and he had learned it the hard way. To see why his words carry so much weight, go back to a cold night in Jerusalem about thirty years before he wrote them. In the olive grove of Gethsemane, soldiers and temple police came with torches to arrest Jesus. Peter, the loyal fisherman, pulled out a sword and cut off the right ear of Malchus, the high priest's servant (John 18:10). Jesus told him to put the sword away and healed the man, then let himself be tied up and led off.

Peter followed from a distance into the courtyard of the high priest's house. John notes that "it was cold, and the servants and officials stood around a fire they had made to keep warm" (John 18:18). Peter stood with them and held out his hands to the coals. Then a servant girl at the gate looked at his face in the firelight and asked, "You aren't one of this man's disciples too, are you?" (John 18:17). He said no. Someone else asked, and he said no again. Then a relative of Malchus, the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said he had seen him in the garden. Mark says Peter "began to call down curses, and he swore to them, 'I don't know this man you're talking about'" (Mark 14:71). A rooster crowed. Across the courtyard, "the Lord turned and looked straight at Peter," and Peter "went outside and wept bitterly" (Luke 22:61–62).

That night Peter answered twice, once with a sword and once with a curse, and fear was behind both answers. One was the fear of losing Jesus, and the other was the fear of being taken along with him. Now fast forward three decades. Peter is an old man, probably in Rome, which he calls "Babylon" (1 Peter 5:13). He is writing to believers scattered across what is now Turkey (1:1). These were ordinary people whose neighbors slandered them, accused them of doing wrong (2:12), and made life costly for them because they followed Jesus. In chapter 3 he speaks first to wives with unbelieving husbands, then to husbands, and then to everyone: "Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult. On the contrary, repay evil with blessing" (3:9). Then he quotes the prophet Isaiah: "Do not fear their threats; do not be frightened" (3:14). After that comes the verse many Christians have memorized:

"But in your hearts revere Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience, so that those who speak maliciously against your good behavior in Christ may be ashamed of their slander." (1 Peter 3:15–16)

Read in light of the courtyard, almost every phrase looks like a scar that has healed. The word for "answer" is the Greek apologia, a courtroom word for a reasoned defense. Peter's own trial took place beside a fire outside a courtroom, and he had no defense to give. "Everyone who asks" would include a servant girl at a gate. The word for "gentleness," praütēs, was used of strength under control, like a strong horse that has been trained to respond to a light touch. Jesus used the same family of words for himself when he said, "I am gentle and humble in heart" (Matthew 11:29). The man who once swung a sword in the dark now asks the church to answer gently.

The word Peter uses for "respect" is even more striking. It is phobos, the ordinary Greek word for fear. One way to read the passage is that Peter is moving fear to its proper place. In verse 14 he tells his readers not to fear what people threaten. In verse 15 he tells them to carry a holy fear, a deep reverence before God that makes them careful and humble with everyone else. Fear of people made Peter lie. Reverence for Christ would make him brave and kind.

Peter also puts his instructions in a particular order. The words "in your hearts revere Christ as Lord" echo Isaiah 8:13, where the prophet says, "The LORD Almighty is the one you are to regard as holy." Peter quotes it and puts Christ where Isaiah had written the LORD, which is a bold statement of who he believed Jesus to be. The verb means to set apart as holy, to give someone the throne. In the courtyard Jesus was standing only yards away, but fear was ruling Peter's heart. The ready answer starts on the inside, with the question of who sits on the throne, long before a word is spoken.

Peter knew this because of a second fire. After the resurrection, Jesus waited for his discouraged friends on the shore of Galilee beside "a fire of burning coals" (John 21:9). The Greek word for a charcoal fire, anthrakia, appears in the New Testament only here and in the high priest's courtyard. Beside those coals Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved him, once for each denial, and Peter finally said, "Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you" (John 21:17). The man who failed the first test of his answer was given another chance by a charcoal fire, and he spent the rest of his life practicing what he learned there.

Most of us will never face a soldier's torch. Our questions come at a family reunion, when a tito teases you about still going to church, or in the office pantry, when a co-worker asks how you stayed calm after the layoffs. They come from a classmate who wonders why you bow your head before eating at Jollibee. For some, they come from a spouse who does not believe, and Peter tells those wives that a husband may be "won over without words" by the way they live (3:1). Often our lives answer before our lips do. Even so, Peter wants us ready, and that kind of readiness can be learned. This week you could write down two or three plain sentences explaining why you have hope, using your own story of what Jesus has done for you, and then ask God for the chance to share them kindly.

When the moment comes, answer the way McCain answered that woman in Lakeville: firmly about the truth, and gently and respectfully toward the person in front of you. Do not use a sword or a sneer, and do not try to win the argument at the cost of the person. Hope that has set Christ apart in the heart can afford to speak softly. If you remember times you stayed silent, or answered with sharp words, remember the reason Peter gives in the very next verse: "For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God" (3:18). He brought Peter from the courtyard to the shore, and he can do the same for you. Your next answer can be the gentle one.

articles.title: The Breath the Bones Were Waiting For
articles.dek: In Ezekiel's valley, the bodies were whole and still not alive. A doctor's discovery about newborn lungs helps explain what God did next.
articles.quote: Every bone can be back in place and a life can still be waiting for breath, and breath is the one thing God has promised to give.
articles.body:
In the late 1950s, a young American pediatrician named Mary Ellen Avery kept returning to the same heartbreaking puzzle. Premature babies were dying of something doctors called hyaline membrane disease, and the deaths made little sense. These infants were born with everything in place, from tiny fingers to beating hearts to lungs that were fully formed. Yet within hours of birth they began to struggle for air, their small chests pulling harder with every breath until many of them simply wore out.

Working at Harvard with the physiologist Jere Mead, Avery studied lung tissue from babies who had died and found what was missing. Healthy lungs are coated with a slippery substance called surfactant, which keeps the millions of tiny air sacs from collapsing each time a person breathes out. Without it, every breath is like blowing up a brand new balloon from scratch. Their 1959 paper changed the question doctors were asking, because the babies had the whole structure for breathing and lacked only the thing that let a breath stay.

The hopeful chapter came two decades later and half a world away. In 1980, a Japanese doctor named Tetsuro Fujiwara gave premature infants a surfactant preparation drawn from cow lungs, and their breathing eased within hours. By the 1990s surfactant therapy had become a standard tool in neonatal intensive care units around the world, including hospitals here in the Philippines. Many Filipino parents who have stood outside a NICU window, watching a baby born weeks too early, owe part of their joy to a doctor who refused to accept that a fully formed body had to be a breathless one.

Long before anyone owned a microscope, a prophet named Ezekiel saw a valley full of bodies with exactly that problem. To understand why the vision mattered so much, it helps to know where Ezekiel was standing when he saw it.

Ezekiel was a priest who had been carried off to Babylon in 597 BC, one of thousands of Judeans marched away from home. For years he warned his fellow exiles that Jerusalem would fall, and in Ezekiel 33:21 the news finally arrived through a survivor: "The city has fallen!" The temple had been burned, and King Zedekiah had been blinded and led away in chains. The people's response is recorded in Ezekiel 37:11, and it may be the most honest sentence of despair in the Old Testament: "Our bones are dried up and our hope is gone; we are cut off."

God answered that sentence with a vision. "The hand of the LORD was on me," Ezekiel writes, "and he brought me out by the Spirit of the LORD and set me in the middle of a valley; it was full of bones" (Ezekiel 37:1). He led the prophet "back and forth among them," and Ezekiel saw "a great many bones on the floor of the valley, bones that were very dry" (37:2). The law warned priests against making themselves unclean through contact with the dead (Leviticus 21:1), so this was a place Ezekiel's whole training would have taught him to avoid. God walked him through it slowly anyway, close enough to see how long these people had been gone.

Then came the question: "Son of man, can these bones live?" Ezekiel gave the wisest answer a person can give in the presence of something that looks hopeless: "Sovereign LORD, you alone know" (37:3). God told him to preach to the bones, and as he did, the valley began to rattle. The bones came together, "bone to bone," and then tendons and flesh appeared on them and skin covered them (37:7–8). It must have been an astonishing sight, a field of skeletons becoming a field of bodies. And then the vision pauses on one unsettling detail, "but there was no breath in them" (37:8), so God gave a second command.

Then he said to me, "Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and say to it, 'This is what the Sovereign LORD says: Come, breath, from the four winds and breathe into these slain, that they may live.'" So I prophesied as he commanded me, and breath entered them; they came to life and stood up on their feet, a vast army. (Ezekiel 37:9–10)

English translators need three different words to carry what Ezekiel wrote with one. The Hebrew word ruach can mean breath, wind, or spirit, and it runs through this chapter like a thread. It is the ruach of the LORD that carries Ezekiel into the valley (37:1), the ruach the bodies lack (37:8), the four winds the prophet summons (37:9), and finally God's own ruach in the promise that explains the whole vision: "I will put my Spirit in you and you will live" (37:14). Any Israelite hearing this would have thought of Genesis 2:7, where God formed the first man from dust and then "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Ezekiel's valley is creation happening a second time.

The vision also opens up the chapter before it. In Ezekiel 36:26–27, God had promised, "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you... And I will put my Spirit in you." The valley turns that promise into a picture. One way to read the two stages of the miracle is this: God would restore the shape of Israel's life, bringing them home and rebuilding their towns, and that would be good. Yet structure by itself could never make them live. Like the premature babies in Mary Ellen Avery's lab, they could have every part in place and still be unable to hold a breath, and life would come only when God breathed into them himself.

Most of us know people who are living somewhere between verse 8 and verse 10. A family still eats dinner together on Sundays, but no one really talks. A marriage keeps its routines while the warmth has quietly drained out of it, or a friend attends every gathering and smiles in every photo, yet alone at night says something close to Ezekiel 37:11. The bones are all in place, and the breath is missing.

When we meet that kind of dryness, our instinct is to work on the bones. We offer advice, adjust schedules, and suggest a better job or a new routine. Those things matter, and God himself put the bones together first. Still, the vision suggests that our deepest help for a dry person comes through the two things God asked of Ezekiel. He walked the prophet back and forth among the bones before he ever asked him to speak, and relational wisdom begins there, with the patience to stay close to someone's sorrow long enough to see how dry it really is, without rushing to tidy it up. Then God told Ezekiel to speak twice, once to the bones and once to the breath. The prophet could announce God's word, but only God could send the wind, so Ezekiel's second sermon was really a prayer spoken out loud.

That humble answer in verse 3 belongs here too. "You alone know" protects us from the two errors that most often hurt the people we love, which are pretending we can fix them and quietly giving up on them. Ezekiel had no idea whether those bones could live, so he left that question with God and kept speaking until the valley stood up.

The rest of the chapter shows how far God's breath reaches. In 37:15–23, Ezekiel takes two sticks, one labeled for Judah and one for the northern tribes, two halves of a family that had been divided for more than three centuries. God tells him, "Join them together into one stick so that they will become one in your hand" (37:17). The same Spirit who raises the dead also reconciles brothers who stopped speaking long ago, which is a deeply hopeful detail for anyone carrying a broken relationship with a sibling or a parent.

Think of one person in your life whose hope seems to have dried up. Sometime this week, walk among it with them by calling or visiting, asking how they really are, and listening without trying to repair anything. Then, when you pray, speak to the breath on their behalf, asking God by name to put his Spirit in them so they may live, and look for one sentence of life you can say to them in person. You may not see the valley stand up right away, just as NICU nurses sometimes wait days before a tiny chest begins to rise steadily on its own.

God has made a promise about valleys like this one, and he signed it with his own name: "Then you will know that I the LORD have spoken, and I have done it, declares the LORD" (37:14). Every bone can be back in place and a life can still be waiting for breath, and breath is the one thing God has promised to give. So keep walking among the dry places in the people you love and keep speaking to the wind on their behalf, because the God who breathed into dust in Eden is still breathing today.

articles.title: Where the Eyes Go
articles.dek: Psalm 123 was sung by people worn out from being looked down on. It shows them, and us, where to lift our eyes.
articles.quote: When the proud look down on you, lift your eyes to the One whose looking down is always mercy.
articles.body:
When the journalist Euny Hong moved with her family from the United States to Seoul as a young girl, she found that her new classmates seemed to have a sense she lacked. They could walk into a room and know within moments who was upset, who was in charge, and what was about to happen next. Koreans have a word for this ability: nunchi. It is made of two small parts, nun, meaning "eye," and chi, roughly meaning "measure." Nunchi is the art of measuring a room with your eyes, of reading the faint signals in a face or a pause before anyone says a word. Hong later wrote a whole book about it, and she describes it warmly, as a quiet attentiveness that helps people treat one another with care.

Filipinos understand nunchi without ever needing the word. We call it pakiramdam. It is the child who knows from one glance across the dinner table that Mama wants her to stop talking, and the guest who senses exactly when to say, "Sige po, mauna na ako." It is a lovely gift, and it has kept many of us gracious in crowded homes and offices. Yet anyone who has lived by it for long also knows its weariness. When your eyes are always reading other people's faces, you feel every flicker of disapproval, and the faces of those who look down on you can follow you home at night.

Psalm 123 was written by someone who knew that weariness well. In four short verses, it takes the same habit of watchful eyes and gives it a better place to rest.

The psalm belongs to a group of fifteen called the "songs of ascents" (Psalms 120 to 134). Many scholars believe pilgrims sang them as they walked up to Jerusalem for the great festivals. The city sits high in the hill country, so every journey there was a climb, and families sang to keep their hearts steady on the road. Psalm 123 is so brief that it could be sung in under a minute, the kind of song a tired traveler can carry without a book.

It opens with a single voice: "I lift up my eyes to you, to you who sit enthroned in heaven" (Psalm 123:1). By the next verse the singer is saying "our eyes," as if they have turned to the people walking beside them and invited them in. Only near the end do we learn why they are singing at all: "Have mercy on us, LORD, have mercy on us, for we have endured no end of contempt. We have endured no end of ridicule from the arrogant, of contempt from the proud" (Psalm 123:3–4).

We do not know the exact occasion of the psalm. Many readers hear in it the years after the exile, when the Jewish people came home from Babylon to a ruined city and tried to rebuild it while their neighbors laughed. Nehemiah records an official named Sanballat jeering, "What are those feeble Jews doing?" (Nehemiah 4:2). Nehemiah's own prayer in that moment sounds almost exactly like this song: "Hear us, our God, for we are despised" (Nehemiah 4:4). These were people trying to do something good for God, and the scorn would not stop.

"As the eyes of slaves look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a female slave look to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the LORD our God, till he shows us his mercy." (Psalm 123:2)

Commentators often picture a household servant standing quietly at the edge of a room during a meal. In many ancient homes, a servant waited for a small gesture more than a spoken order: a lifted finger for more water, a slight motion toward the door. The servant's eyes stayed on that hand because everything came from it, including direction for the day, food for the evening, protection from harm, and pardon after a mistake. One way to read this verse is as nunchi pointed upward. The psalmist takes the very skill that the scornful had been draining, the constant reading of faces, and gives it a single, steady focus.

Two Hebrew words open the psalm even further. The word translated "arrogant" in verse 4 is sha'ananim, which literally means "those who are at ease," the comfortable and untroubled. The contempt came from people who had never had to climb anything, who could look down from their comfort at those still struggling up the hill. The word for mercy in verse 3 is chanan, which means to show favor, to bend toward someone in kindness when they have nothing to offer in return. In Hebrew the cry is only a few syllables, chonnenu YHWH chonnenu, the kind of prayer a person can breathe on a steep road.

This suggests something tender about the picture. The proud look down on the pilgrims with contempt. The God who sits "enthroned in heaven" is higher than any of them, so he looks down too, yet his looking down is chanan, the downward bend of grace. When the proud look down on you, lift your eyes to the One whose looking down is always mercy.

The small word "till" in verse 2 matters as well. The psalm ends with the eyes still lifted and the mercy still coming, and its final line is about the contempt the people have endured. Scripture lets the waiting be honest. Yet the pilgrims sang this song and kept walking, and the very next song in the collection begins, "If the LORD had not been on our side" (Psalm 124:1). The answer to Psalm 123 is waiting a few steps further up the road.

Where are your eyes resting this week? Perhaps on the relative who greets you at every reunion with "Ang taba mo na" or "Kailan ka mag-aasawa?" Perhaps on the coworker who smiles a little too long at your accent, or on the comments under something you shared online. Pakiramdam reads every one of them, and some of those faces can stay with you for days, long after the people themselves have forgotten what they said.

The psalm offers a simple practice. When you catch yourself replaying someone's scornful look, lift your eyes for a moment, even literally, toward the sky or the ceiling, and pray the short prayer of verse 3: "Have mercy on us, LORD, have mercy on us." Pray it in the plural, as the pilgrims did, and let it include the others in your life who are being looked down on too. You will still notice people's faces, because that is how God made you, but you will be choosing which face gets the final word.

You do not need to lose your pakiramdam to follow this psalm. It is a gift worth keeping, and here it finds its truest home: in the steady watching of a hand that has never once withheld kindness from those who look to it. The road may still be uphill today, and the voices of the comfortable may still carry. Keep singing as you climb, keep your eyes on the One enthroned above it all, and trust that his hand is already turning toward you in mercy.

articles.title: The Fire That Keeps the Silver
articles.dek: Hezekiah's scribes copied a proverb about dross while their king was cleaning out the temple. It shows what God is doing when the heat comes, and who He believes you can become.
articles.quote: The silversmith skims away the dross because he has already decided the silver is worth keeping.
articles.body:
Walk into one of the small silver workshops in Baguio on a cool amihan morning and you will often find a craftsman bent over a small flame, holding a crucible no bigger than a coffee cup at the end of his tongs. The city has been known for its silver filigree for generations, and many of the hands that twist those fine wires learned the trade from a parent or an uncle at the same kind of worn wooden bench. Before any earring or brooch can be shaped, the metal has to be melted. As the silver turns liquid, a dull gray skin creeps across the surface, a crust of oxides and stray metals that had been hiding inside scrap that looked perfectly clean. The silversmith skims it off with a patient flick of a rod, waits a moment, and skims again.

Ask him whether he worries about losing silver in the fire and he will probably smile at the question. The fire is how he keeps his silver. What he scrapes away was never going to become anything beautiful, and what remains is finally pure enough to take the shape he already has in mind. A strand of filigree is so fine in places that a single fleck of impurity would make it snap under the pliers, so every pass of the skimming rod is an act of care for a piece that does not exist yet.

Proverbs 25 opens with an unusual editor's note: "These are more proverbs of Solomon, compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah" (Proverbs 25:1). Solomon had been dead for more than two centuries when Hezekiah came to the throne, around 715 years before Christ. Hezekiah's father, Ahaz, had shut the doors of the temple and filled Jerusalem with altars to other gods. According to 2 Chronicles, Hezekiah reopened those doors in the very first month of his reign and gave the Levites a blunt order: "Remove all defilement from the sanctuary" (2 Chronicles 29:5). The priests went in, "brought out to the courtyard of the LORD's temple everything unclean that they found," and the Levites hauled it all down to the Kidron Valley (2 Chronicles 29:16). It was a national cleanup, carried out one cartload at a time.

This is the setting in which the king's scribes sat down with Solomon's old sayings, copying and arranging them for a new generation. In the same city, the prophet Isaiah was preaching a message from God that used the image of a silversmith: "I will thoroughly purge away your dross and remove all your impurities" (Isaiah 1:25). It is easy to imagine those scribes reaching the lines below and recognizing their own week in them.

"Remove the dross from the silver, and a silversmith can produce a vessel; remove wicked officials from the king's presence, and his throne will be established through righteousness." (Proverbs 25:4–5)

The Hebrew makes the parallel even tighter than the English. Both halves of the proverb begin with the same word, hago, a verb meaning to drive out or separate. The dross is sigim, the scum that rises off molten metal, and the silversmith is a tsoreph, literally "one who refines." Solomon sets the workshop and the palace side by side and lets the first explain the second. Impurity is removed, and only then can something useful be formed, a keli, a vessel fit to be held and filled. In the same way, corrupt advisers are removed from the king's presence, and only then does his rule stand firm. The order matters in both pictures. The beautiful thing comes after the separation and grows out of it.

One way to read this proverb, especially beside Isaiah, is to hear the hope folded inside it. A silversmith never puts worthless rock into his crucible. He melts down silver because he already knows its value, and the heat he applies is measured against the shape he intends to make. The silversmith skims away the dross because he has already decided the silver is worth keeping. When the prophet Malachi later described God's work among His people, he chose the same posture: "He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver" (Malachi 3:3). A refiner who sits is a refiner who stays at the bench, watching the metal closely until the work is finished.

That changes how a believer can understand the hard seasons. Many of us experience the heat of life, a failure exposed, a friendship that ended, a long wait for an answer, as evidence that God has set us aside. Proverbs 25 suggests the opposite reading. The heat is often the moment when what was hidden in us finally floats to the surface where it can be seen, named, and lifted away. Pride we never noticed, bitterness we had dressed up as being realistic, a habit of quiet dishonesty that seemed harmless, these rise to the top under pressure. They rise there so the Refiner can take them off.

The gospel takes the picture one step further. Isaiah, preaching in Hezekiah's Jerusalem, also looked ahead to a coming King who would "reign on David's throne and over his kingdom, establishing and upholding it with justice and righteousness from that time on and forever" (Isaiah 9:7). Proverbs 25:5 describes a throne established through righteousness, and the New Testament shows us how that throne was finally secured. Jesus did more than stand beside the crucible and skim. He went into the fire Himself on our behalf, because "God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21). The impurity that should have ruined the silver was carried away in His body on the cross. Every refining we experience now is the outworking of a rescue already finished, which is why Paul could write with confidence that "he who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus" (Philippians 1:6).

The second half of the proverb also offers a very practical question for today. Every heart has a throne, and every throne has advisers standing near it. In ancient Judah, the wicked officials were the voices that whispered in the king's ear, shaping his decisions while appearing loyal. Our advisers today look more ordinary: the group chat that makes cynicism feel normal, the late-night scrolling that leaves us envious and restless, the old resentment we consult before we answer someone, the voice that tells us a small compromise will not matter. None of them wear a sign announcing they are corrupt, which is exactly why they stay so long in the room.

Hezekiah's reform began with a single act of opening the doors and letting light into rooms that had been shut. You can begin in a similarly simple way. Before you sleep tonight, ask God to show you one voice that has been standing too close to your decisions, and then take one concrete step to move it farther from the throne, whether that means muting a thread, deleting an app for a season, or confessing a grudge to a trusted friend. It will feel small, and it may even feel like losing something. Remember the craftsman in Baguio, patient over his little flame, lifting away the gray crust so the bright metal underneath can finally shine.

You are silver in the hands of a Refiner who sits down to do His work, and He has never once been careless with what He loves. Whatever heat you are feeling this week, He is watching closely, He knows exactly what He is making, and He intends to finish it. Let Him skim away what was never really you, and trust that what remains will be shaped into a vessel worth holding, ready to be filled and carried out into the world for His glory.
